a OurBigBook.com
For a continuously differentiable vector field u on a bounded region V⊂R3 with piecewise smooth closed boundary S=∂V, the divergence theorem states
∫V​∇⋅udV=∫S​u⋅n^dS=∫S​u⋅dS.​
(1)
Here ∇⋅u is its divergence, dV is the volume element, dS is the surface area element, n^ is the outward unit normal, and dS=n^dS. Thus a volume integral of the divergence equals the outward flux through the boundary.

Since a is constant, the product rule gives ∇⋅(aψ)=a⋅∇ψ. Applying the divergence theorem therefore gives
a⋅∫V​∇ψdV=∫S​ψa⋅dS=a⋅∫S​ψdS.
(2)
This holds for every constant vector a, so each component of the difference vanishes. Consequently the gradient has the boundary representation
∫V​∇ψdV=∫S​ψdS.​
(3)

−a⋅∫V​∇×AdV=−a⋅∫S​n^×AdS.
(4)

∫V​∇×AdV=∫S​n^×AdS.​

Use Einstein summation convention and write ∂j​=∇j​. Since ∂j​ri​=δij​, where δij​ is the Kronecker delta, the product rule gives
∂j​(ri​wj​)=δij​wj​+ri​∂j​wj​=wi​+Pi​.
(6)
This proves Pi​=∂j​(ri​wj​)−wi​​. Now take wj​=∂j​ψ. Integrating this identity and applying the divergence theorem to the first term gives
∫V​ri​∇2ψdV=∫S​ri​∂j​ψdSj​−∫V​∂i​ψdV.
(7)
Part (b) changes the last volume integral of the gradient into a surface integral, yielding
∫V​ri​∇2ψdV=∫S​ri​∂j​ψdSj​−∫S​ψdSi​.​
(8)
Here dSi​=n^i​dS; the Laplacian is ∇2ψ=∂j​∂j​ψ.

Apply the product rule to the tensor field, without assuming any symmetry of Σ:
∂j​(ri​∂k​Σkj​)=δij​∂k​Σkj​+ri​∂j​∂k​Σkj​=∂k​Σki​+ri​∂j​∂k​Σkj​.

Apply separation of variables with ρ(x,t)=X(x)T(t) and temporal factor T=e−λt. The spatial eigenvalue equation is
−DX′′−γX=λX,X(0)=X(L)=0.
(14)
The nontrivial solutions of these Dirichlet boundary conditions are sine eigenfunctions. Normalizing in the usual inner product on (0,L) gives
ψn​(x)=L2​​sinLnπx​,λn​=D(Lnπ​)2−γ,n=1,2,…,​
(15)
with ∫0L​ψn​ψm​dx=δnm​. The superposition principle and the Fourier sine series then give
ρ(x,t)=n=1∑∞​an​L2​​sinLnπx​exp[(γ−L2Dn2π2​)t].​
(16)
The constants are the initial-data coefficients an​=∫0L​ρ(x,0)ψn​(x)dx. Here physical diffusion means D>0.

b OurBigBook.com
By orthogonality and the sampling property of the Dirac delta distribution,
an​=ρ0​∫0L​δ(x−x0​)ψn​(x)dx=ρ0​L2​​sinLnπx0​​​.
(17)
Consequently the reaction-diffusion equation solution is
ρ(x,t)=L2ρ0​​n=1∑∞​sinLnπx0​​sinLnπx​exp[(γ−L2Dn2π2​)t].​
(18)
For every t>0 this eigenfunction expansion is smoothed by the Gaussian decay in n. As t↓0, it recovers the specified initial condition in the sense of distributions.

Solution

Words: 102
c OurBigBook.com
The smallest decay-rate eigenvalue is λ1​=Dπ2/L2−γ, so the threshold is
γc​(D,L)=L2Dπ2​.​
(19)
Because 0<x0​<L, a1​>0. For every fixed interior point 0<x<L, the first sine eigenfunction is positive and the remaining terms have strictly faster decay relative to it. Hence
ρ(x,t)∼L2ρ0​​sinLπx0​​sinLπx​e(γ−γc​)t.
(20)
One can justify the relative-error limit directly: after factoring out the first exponential, the absolute remainder is bounded by (2ρ0​/L)∑n≥2​e−Dπ2(n2−1)t/L2, which tends to zero. Thus ρ→0 if γ<γc​​, and ρ(x,t)→+∞ for each interior x if γ>γc​​. The boundary values stay zero. At equality the first term is stationary and the density approaches its positive sine profile.

d

Words: 118 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 118
d OurBigBook.com
Let f(x)=ρ(x,0). The first normalized Fourier sine series coefficient is
a1​=L2​​∫0L​f(x)sinLπx​dx>0.
(21)
Strict positivity follows because f≥0, has positive total mass, and sin(πx/L)>0 everywhere inside the interval. In particular, there is no cancellation that could remove the slowest term. This is the positivity of the first Dirichlet reaction-diffusion coefficient.
For finite initial mass M=∫0L​f(x)dx, all coefficients satisfy ∣an​∣≤2/L​M. The eigenfunction expansion therefore gives the uniform bound
​eλ1​tρ(x,t)−a1​ψ1​(x)​≤L2M​∑n=2∞​e−Dπ2(n2−1)t/L2⟶0.
(22)
The positive first profile thus controls the long-time behavior. We recover exactly the threshold γc​=Dπ2/L2​, with decay below it and unbounded positive growth at every interior point above it. The finite-mass condition is the usual meaning of an initial density profile here; standard positive-time smoothing gives the same conclusion in the usual broader admissible data classes.

For an exponential trial y=erx, the characteristic equation is
r2+2ar+a2+b2=(r+a)2+b2=0.
(23)
Its distinct complex roots are r=−a±ib. Thus the general real solution of the homogeneous second-order linear differential equation is
yh​(x)=e−ax[C1​cos(bx)+C2​sin(bx)].​
(24)
The two displayed solutions have nonzero Wronskian be−2ax and hence linear independence. The same formula permits complex solutions when C1​,C2​ are complex.

ii

Words: 120 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
ii OurBigBook.com
For the zero-data initial value problem, choose a causal Green function satisfying Lx​G(x,ξ)=δ(x−ξ) and G=0 for x<ξ. Continuity at x=ξ prevents a derivative of the Dirac delta distribution, while integration across the source gives
G(ξ+,ξ)=0,∂x​G(ξ+,ξ)−∂x​G(ξ−,ξ)=1.
(25)
For x>ξ, part (i) gives the shifted homogeneous solutions. The zero value at the join removes the cosine term, and the unit derivative jump fixes the sine coefficient. Therefore the causal Green function of a damped oscillator is
G(x,ξ)=⎩⎨⎧​b1​e−a(x−ξ)sin[b(x−ξ)],0,​x≥ξ,x<ξ.​​
(26)
Equivalently, multiply the first expression by the Heaviside step function H(x−ξ). The required solution is
y(x)=∫0∞​G(x,ξ)g(ξ)dξ=b1​∫0x​e−a(x−ξ)sin[b(x−ξ)]g(ξ)dξ.​
(27)
Its initial value and first derivative vanish: the interval has zero length at x=0 and the kernel vanishes at its upper limit. Differentiating twice shows that the upper-limit contribution to y′′ is precisely g(x), while the remaining homogeneous kernel terms cancel in Ly.

The original PDF has the absolute-value hypothesis ∣g(ξ)∣<Ce−sξ, which is missing from the local OCR. From the Green's function formula and ∣sin∣≤1,
∣y(x)∣​≤bC​∫0x​e−a(x−ξ)e−sξdξ=bC​e−ax∫0x​e−(s−a)ξdξ=b(s−a)C​e−ax[1−e−(s−a)x]≤b(s−a)C​e−ax.​
(28)
Because s>a>0, the upper bound tends to zero. The squeeze theorem proves y(x)→0 as x→∞​.

Let Av=λv with v=0. Taking the Hermitian inner product with v gives v†Av=λ∥v∥2. For an anti-Hermitian matrix,
v†Av=v†A†v=−v†Av.
(37)
Consequently λ∥v∥2=−λ∥v∥2. As ∥v∥2>0, the eigenvalue satisfies λ=−λ​, or λ=iθ with θ∈R​. Zero is included as a purely imaginary eigenvalue.

b OurBigBook.com
If I+A were a singular matrix, a nonzero vector v would satisfy (I+A)v=0, so Av=−v. This would make −1 an eigenvalue of the anti-Hermitian matrix, contrary to part (a). Thus I+A is invertible​. The same argument shows I−A is an invertible matrix, which will also be used below.

c OurBigBook.com
Taking the conjugate transpose term by term in the convergent matrix exponential gives
U†=eA†=e−A.
(38)
The matrices A and −A commute, so the matrix exponential product law gives U†U=e−AeA=I and likewise UU†=I. Hence U is unitary​.
For V, use the inverse and product rules for the conjugate transpose:
V†=[(I+A)−1]†(I−A)†=(I−A)−1(I+A).
(39)
The factors I±A commute, as do their inverses, since they are expressions in the same matrix. Consequently
V†V=(I−A)−1(I+A)(I−A)(I+A)−1=I,
(40)
and similarly VV†=I. Therefore V is unitary​. This rational construction is the skew-Hermitian form of the Cayley transform of a Hermitian matrix, obtained by writing A=iH with H a Hermitian matrix.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Choose a real unit eigenvector e1​ of the real symmetric matrix Q, with eigenvalue λ1​. Its orthogonal complement is an invariant subspace: for any v with e1T​v=0,
e1T​Qv=(Qe1​)Tv=λ1​e1T​v=0.
(45)
The restriction of Q to this (n−1)-dimensional space is again real and symmetric. Applying the same argument inductively produces an orthonormal basis e1​,…,en​ of real eigenvectors. The base case n=1 is immediate. This proves the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices without assuming that distinct eigenvalues are available.
One can also check that eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal: λi​eiT​ej​=(Qei​)Tej​=eiT​Qej​=λj​eiT​ej​. Within a repeated eigenspace, the Gram-Schmidt process preserves the eigenvector property. Thus repeated eigenvalues cause no obstruction, and Q=ODOT for an orthogonal O and real diagonal D​.

x2+(y−P2−1b(P2+1)​)2=(P2−1)24b2P2​.

For the upper Apollonius circle, let its constant ratio be P>1. Matching the center and radius from part (i) gives
y0​=P2−1b(P2+1)​,R=P2−12bP​.
(58)
Subtracting their squares yields b=y02​−R2​​. Also
Ry0​​=2P+P−1​=cosh(logP),logP=arcosh(y0​/R).
(59)
The relevant inverse hyperbolic cosine is positive. Now log∣(z+ib)/(z−ib)∣ is the real part of a local holomorphic logarithm, hence a harmonic function away from z=±ib. The point ib is inside the excluded disk, because 0<y0​−b<R, while −ib is below the real axis. Thus neither singularity lies in the physical domain.
On y=0 the numerator and denominator have equal modulus, so the logarithm is zero. On the circular boundary its value is logP=arcosh(y0​/R). Therefore the harmonic potential between a grounded line and a circular boundary is
V(x,y)=arcosh(y0​/R)V0​​log​x+iy−iy02​−R2​x+iy+iy02​−R2​​​.​
(60)
This verifies Laplace's equation and both prescribed Dirichlet boundary conditions. It also tends to zero at infinity. A uniqueness assertion on this unbounded domain would require an additional boundedness or infinity condition; the displayed function is the natural decaying solution requested.

For real z>0, apply integration by parts to the gamma integral with u=tz and dv=e−tdt:
Γ(z+1)=∫0∞​tze−tdt=[−tze−t]0∞​+z∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt.
(62)
The boundary term vanishes: tz→0 at zero, and exponential decay dominates the power at infinity. This proves the Gamma function recurrence
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z).​
(63)

Solution
Words: 74
iii OurBigBook.com
Iterating the Gamma function recurrence gives a meromorphic continuation
Γ(z)=z(z+1)⋯(z+m)Γ(z+m+1)​,m=0,1,2,….
(64)
Near z=−m, the numerator is analytic and tends to Γ(1)=1. Exactly one denominator factor, z+m, vanishes, while all other factors tend to the nonzero product (−1)mm!. Therefore
Γ(z)∼m!(−1)m​z+m1​.
(65)
Thus z=0,−1,−2,… are all simple poles​. More precisely, the Gamma function residue at a nonpositive integer is Resz=−m​Γ(z)=(−1)m/m!​. Taking m large enough to put z+m+1 in the original right half-plane also shows that this continuation introduces no other finite poles.

First simplify the coefficient of y using
x−mm3​+x2+mx+m2=x−mx3​.
(66)
After dividing by x(x−m), the second-order linear differential equation is
y′′+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0,P(x)=x1​+x−m1​,Q(x)=(x−m)2ω2x2​.
(67)
At zero, xP→1 and x2Q→0, and both products are analytic there. At m, (x−m)P→1 and (x−m)2Q→m2ω2, again with analytic extensions. Thus x=0 and x=m are regular singular points​, and there are no other finite singular points.
Infinity must also be considered because the question asks for all singular points. Put t=1/x and Y(t)=y(1/t). The coefficient of Y in its normal-form equation is Q(1/t)/t4∼ω2/t4. Multiplication by t2 does not make it analytic at zero. Hence x=∞ is an irregular singular point​.

Set t=x−m and use the Frobenius solution y=tν(a0​+a1​t+⋯) with a0​=0. From part (a), the leading coefficients are P∼1/t and Q∼m2ω2/t2. The coefficient of the lowest power tν−2 is therefore
[ν(ν−1)+ν+m2ω2]a0​.
(68)
The indicial equation reduces to ν2+m2ω2=0, giving
ν+​=imω,ν−​=−imω.​
(69)
Since mω>0, the two indicial roots differ by a nonzero imaginary number, not an integer. Thus the two local Frobenius solutions exist independently on a chosen branch of log(x−m).

Define the Wronskian by W=y1​y2′​−y1′​y2​. Differentiating and using the normal-form differential equation gives
W′=y1​y2′′​−y1′′​y2​=−P(x)(y1​y2′​−y1′​y2​)=−P(x)W.
(70)
Integrating this first-order linear differential equation proves Abel's identity:
W(x)=Cexp[−∫xp(u)du],p(u)=u1​+u−m1​.​
(71)
Thus, on any interval avoiding zero and m,
W(x)=x(x−m)C​​.
(72)
Absolute-value signs from real logarithms can be absorbed into the constant on each such interval. For linearly independent solutions, C=0.

At zero the indicial equation is ν(ν−1)+ν=ν2=0, with repeated indicial root zero. To exhibit the analytic solution rather than only its candidate exponent, clear the denominator in the normal form:
x(x−m)2y′′+(2x−m)(x−m)y′+ω2x3y=0.
(73)
Substitute y1​=∑n≥0​bn​xn and equate coefficients. With bj​=0 for negative indices, the linear recurrence relation is
m2(n+1)2bn+1​=mn(2n+1)bn​−n(n−1)bn−1​−ω2bn−3​,n≥0.​
(74)
Every leading coefficient on the left is nonzero. Hence b0​=0 is free and all later coefficients are determined; the Frobenius method guarantees local convergence up to the next singularity. In particular,
b1​=b2​=b3​=0,b4​=−16m2ω2b0​​,y1​=b0​[1−16m2ω2x4​+O(x5)].
(75)
For a second solution, use reduction of order. Writing y2​=y1​v gives W=y12​v′, so part (c) yields
y2​(x)=y1​(x)∫xs(s−m)y1​(s)2Cds​,C=0.​
(76)
The additive constant in the integral only adds a multiple of y1​. As x↓0 within (0,m), its integrand is
x(x−m)y1​(x)2C​=−mb02​C​x1​+O(1).
(77)
Therefore
y2​(x)=c0​logx+O(1),c0​=−mb0​C​=0.​
(78)
The nonzero Wronskian proves linear independence, and the logarithm is unavoidable for this second local solution.

For fixed initial and final coordinates, the two Euler-Lagrange equations are
dtd​(∂x˙∂f​)−∂x∂f​=0,dtd​(∂y˙​∂f​)−∂y∂f​=0.​
(79)
Indeed the first variation of the functional is
δF=∫0T​(fx​δx+fy​δy+fx˙​δx˙+fy˙​​δy˙​)dt.
(80)
Integration by parts moves the time derivatives from the variations; their endpoint values are zero. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations then gives the two equations above.

Words: 64
b OurBigBook.com
The total derivative contributes only the boundary term
∫0T​dtd​g(x,y)dt=g(x(T),y(T))−g(x(0),y(0)).
(81)
This is fixed by the endpoint data, so its first variation vanishes. It cannot change the Euler-Lagrange equations or which path minimizes F.
For a direct check, let h=gx​x˙+gy​y˙​. Then
dtd​hx˙​=gxx​x˙+gxy​y˙​=hx​,dtd​hy˙​​=gyx​x˙+gyy​y˙​=hy​.
(82)
The equality uses commuting mixed partial derivatives. Thus dg/dt contributes zero to both Euler-Lagrange equations​, as in total time derivatives preserve fixed-endpoint Euler-Lagrange equations.

Words: 103 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 103
c OurBigBook.com
This is an isoperimetric constraint, imposed on the whole path rather than separately at each time. Introduce a constant Lagrange multiplier λ and replace the variational integrand by f​=f+λu. The modified Euler-Lagrange equations are
dtd​fx˙​−fx​−λux​=0,dtd​fy˙​​−fy​−λuy​=0.​
(83)
Solve these together with the fixed endpoint conditions, treating λ as an unknown constant, then choose its value so that
∫0T​u(x(t),y(t))dt=0.​
(84)
The multiplier is constant because there is one scalar integral constraint. A condition imposed at every time would instead call for a time-dependent multiplier. As usual, this multiplier procedure assumes the constraint is regular, so its first variation does not vanish identically on all admissible variations.

(85)
Substitution into the Euler-Lagrange equations gives
αβγ1​x˙+δ1​x¨=αβ(1+γ1​x˙+γ2​y˙​),αβγ2​x˙+δ2​y¨​=0.
(86)
The γ1​ terms cancel in the first equation, leaving
δ1​x¨=αβ(1+γ2​y˙​),δ2​y¨​=−αβγ2​x˙.​
(87)
These are accompanied by x(0)=y(0)=0 and x(T)=y(T)=S. The cancellation is consistent with part (b): the term proportional to γ1​ is the total derivative of αγ1​(x+βx2/2).

fline​=α(1+βx)+α(γ1​+γ2​)(1+βx)x˙+2δ​x˙2.

Its middle term is the total derivative of α(γ1​+γ2​)(x+βx2/2), so it can be dropped for fixed endpoints by part (b). The remaining Euler-Lagrange equation is δx¨=αβ. Integrating twice and imposing x(0)=0, x(T)=S gives
x(t)=y(t)=TS​t−2(δ1​+δ2​)αβ​t(T−t),0≤t≤T.​

This is the unique global minimizer among paths on the specified line. To prove it, add any admissible variation η with η(0)=η(T)=0. The change in fuel, after dropping the fixed boundary term, is
F[x+η]−F[x]=∫0T​[αβη+δx˙η˙​]dt+2δ​∫0T​η˙​2dt=2δ​∫0T​η˙​2dt≥0.

The first integral vanishes by integration by parts and the equation for x. Equality forces η=0. No monotonicity or restriction to the segment between endpoints was imposed in the question; the minimizing coordinate can initially decrease for sufficiently large T.

a OurBigBook.com
Use the standard regular Sturm-Liouville problem hypotheses: positive weight w, real coefficients, and real self-adjoint boundary conditions. The positive weight and boundary-domain assumptions are implicit in the requested real orthonormal basis; real differential coefficients alone would not guarantee them for arbitrary complex boundary conditions.
Multiply the eigenfunction equation by yn​​ and integrate. By self-adjointness, the number ∫ab​yn​​Lyn​dx is real, whereas
∫ab​yn​​Lyn​dx=λn​∫ab​w∣yn​∣2dx.
(91)
The second integral is strictly positive, so λn​∈R​. Because the coefficients and boundary conditions are real, the real and imaginary parts of any complex eigenfunction separately obey the same equation and conditions. At least one is nonzero, so a real eigenfunction can be chosen. More generally, each eigenspace has a real basis, which can be orthonormalized using the weighted inner product.
The orthogonality of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions, with normalization chosen to one, is
∫ab​w(x)ym​(x)​yn​(x)dx=δmn​.​
(92)
For the real choice, omit the complex conjugate.

b

Words: 132 Articles: 1
10 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 132
b OurBigBook.com
The Sturm-Liouville eigenfunction expansion of a suitable real function f is
f(x)=∑n​yn​(x)∫ab​w(ξ)yn​(ξ)f(ξ)dξ=∫ab​[w(ξ)∑n​yn​(ξ)yn​(x)]f(ξ)dξ.
(93)
Comparing this identity with the sampling property of the Dirac delta distribution gives the completeness kernel
w(ξ)n∑​yn​(ξ)yn​(x)=δ(x−ξ).​
(94)
This is an identity of distributions, rather than a pointwise-convergent series of ordinary functions.
Assuming zero is not an eigenvalue, define the spectral Green function of a regular Sturm-Liouville problem by
G(x;ξ)=n∑​λn​yn​(x)yn​(ξ)​.​
(95)
Applying Lx​ gives w(x)∑n​yn​(x)yn​(ξ)=δ(x−ξ): multiplying the preceding completeness kernel by w(x)/w(ξ) leaves the Dirac delta distribution unchanged. Each term also obeys the same homogeneous boundary conditions. There is no extra weight factor in G for the ordinary source measure dξ.
If zero is an eigenvalue, the inverse Green's function does not exist on all forcing functions: the forcing must obey the solvability condition at a Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue. Omitting the zero mode instead constructs a reduced inverse, with its projection removed from the right-hand side. This exception occurs in part (c) at α=1.

c OurBigBook.com
Write the endpoint condition in its linear Robin boundary condition form y′(1)=y(1)/α. For a positive eigenvalue λ=q2, the left Dirichlet boundary condition gives y=Csin(qx), and the right condition gives
qcosq=α1​sinq,tanq=αq.​
(96)
For each positive root qn​, the squared norm is
Nn​=∫01​sin2(qn​x)dx=21​−4qn​sin(2qn​)​.
(97)
Consequently the sine coefficients in any complete expansion are
an​=Nn​∫01​f(x)sin(qn​x)dx​=1−sin(2qn​)/(2qn​)2∫01​f(x)sin(qn​x)dx​.​
(98)
When α>1, these are all modes and the Sturm-Liouville eigenfunction expansion gives exactly the stated sine series, with the usual convergence interpretation. Positivity of all eigenvalues follows from integration by parts and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:
∫01​y(−y′′)dx=∫01​(y′)2dx−αy(1)2​≥(1−α1​)∫01​(y′)2dx>0
(99)
for a nonzero admissible y, since y(1)=∫01​y′dx.
However, the original PDF states only α>0, and with that range its sine-only completeness claim is false. The missing modes are as follows. At α=1, λ=0 admits y=x, so the correct expansion is
f(x)=3x∫01​tf(t)dt+n≥1∑​an​sin(qn​x),α=1.​
(100)
For 0<α<1, a negative eigenvalue λ=−κ2 admits y=sinh(κx), with
tanhκ=ακ,κ>0.​
(101)
There is exactly one positive root: tanhκ/κ decreases strictly from 1 to zero. For example, its derivative has the sign of κsech2κ−tanhκ<0, because sinhκcoshκ>κ. Thus the corrected expansion is
f(x)=a−​sinh(κx)+n≥1∑​an​sin(qn​x),a−​=sinh(2κ)/(4κ)−1/2∫01​f(t)sinh(κt)dt​,0<α<1.​
(102)
These are the nonpositive modes in a Dirichlet-Robin interval expansion. As an explicit counterexample to the printed claim, at α=1 take f(x)=x: it satisfies both boundary conditions, and each positive root obeys
∫01​xsin(qn​x)dx=−qn​cosqn​​+qn2​sinqn​​=0
(103)
because tanqn​=qn​. Thus all an​ vanish despite f=0. Likewise f=sinh(κx) is a counterexample for α<1, by orthogonality of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues. The formulas above give the full solution without silently assuming away the omitted modes.

Put sn​(x)=sin(qn​x) and sm​(x)=sin(qm​x). Their differential equations are −sn′′​=qn2​sn​ and −sm′′​=qm2​sm​. Subtract the two cross-multiplied equations and use integration by parts:
(qn2​−qm2​)∫01​sn​sm​dx=[sn​sm′​−sm​sn′​]01​.
(104)
The lower boundary term is zero because both functions vanish there. At the upper endpoint, the Robin boundary condition gives sj′​(1)=sj​(1)/α, so
sn​(1)sm′​(1)−sm​(1)sn′​(1)=αsn​(1)sm​(1)​−αsm​(1)sn​(1)​=0.
(105)
Since distinct positive roots have qn2​=qm2​, we conclude
∫01​sin(qn​x)sin(qm​x)dx=0,n=m.​
(106)
This orthogonality holds for every α>0, even when the sine family requires the additional nonpositive mode for completeness as explained in part (c).
